messages.subject: Question about phylogenetic partial least squares
parts:
Dear all,

To capture the co-variation among the trait sets in the Procrustes shape, I performed a  phylogenetic PLS (using phylo.integration), which resulted in a strange plot. Certain closely related species appear at both ends of the plot, and all species except for them are clustered in the middle of the plot. Please advise if this is a mathematical problem or something that can be interpreted biologically. 

<R code>
phylo.integration(allometry.phy$GM$pgls.residuals[A , , ],
                                 allometry.phy$GM$pgls.residuals[B , , ],
                                 tree01)

<Results>
r-PLS: 0.955
Effect Size (Z): 3.556
P-value: 0.001

The plot has a phylogenetic tree projected on it, and the colors represent clades.


This is the phylogenetic tree that was used.



 A tree with a mapped continuous character (here, scores in phylo PLS). There is no change in most of the branches. 

Best regards,
Naoto Toyoda

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Question about phylogenetic partial least squares
parts:
Dear Naoto,

PLS is a correlation analysis and the pitfalls of measuring correlation are well-noted on various disciplines.  Here is recent example paper in clinical science, but others can be found for specific disciplines:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5079093/

Here is an example script that covers two problems: range of data and outliers:


> library(phytools)
> library(geomorph)
> set.seed(2003)
> tree <- pbtree(n = 12)
> plot(tree)
> 
> sisters <- c(8, 9) # sister species found in the tree for t11 and t12
> x <- y <- rep(0, 12)
> names(x) <- names(y) <- tree$tip.label
> 
> x[sisters] <- c(-0.1, 0.1)
> y[sisters] <- c(-0.2, 0.3)
> 
> PLS <- phylo.integration(x, y, phy = tree)

Random PLS calculations: 1000 permutations.
  |=============================================================================| 100%

> PLS

Call:
phylo.integration(A = x, A2 = y, phy = tree) 



r-PLS: 1

Effect Size (Z): 3.0727

P-value: 0.008

Based on 1000 random permutations
> plot(PLS, label = tree$tip.label)


This example should demonstrate that a whole lot of nothing going on can produce impressive results.  I simulated data to be practically 0 for every taxon (all were 0, two were tweaked to be practically 0).  This seems plausible with your phylogeny with trait values mapped, showing mostly invariance among all taxa.  The values that were near 0 in my simulation but not quite 0 — i.e., not the same as all others — appear to be outliers even though the range of data suggests all taxa could be considered to have practically the same value.

In other words, a correlation analysis is not warranted.

The problem above is also exacerbated by small sample size, which it appears you have.  One other clue in your data is that the estimated ancestral states are all rather clumped near 0, 0, suggesting there simply is no signal in your data to consider.  It appears all of your taxa have approximately the same shape, at least after accounting for phylogeny.

Hope that helps!

Mike

Dear Professor Michael Collyer,

Thank you for a clear example.
From the example you gave, I understood that even when there is little change between traits, the correlation coefficient is statistically high.
I have two questions.

In PLS2, I got a not strange plot (i.e., not a centralized clusters plot) as I saw in PLS1. Is it correct to assume that PLS2 captures the "biological reality" of co-variation between traits, even though the value of the correlation coefficient is weaker than PLS1, or is this way of interpretation too simplistic, since PLS2 is constrained to be orthogonal to PLS1?

When I excluded one of the two species that were at both ends of the PLS1 plot from my analysis, I did not observe any clusters in PLS1. In other words, could the clusters seen in this case be artificial, originating from taxon sampling, etc.?　 Incidentally, the shape change captured by PLS1 (except for one species) is similar to the shape change captured by PLS2 in the previous case.

Sincerely,
Naoto Toyoda

parts: Dear Naoto,

In PLS2, I got a not strange plot (i.e., not a centralized clusters plot) as I saw in PLS1. Is it correct to assume that PLS2 captures the "biological reality" of co-variation between traits, even though the value of the correlation coefficient is weaker than PLS1, or is this way of interpretation too simplistic, since PLS2 is constrained to be orthogonal to PLS1?

No, in absolutely no way should you feel an urge to interpret the second PLS axes as the biological reality after your first axes have proven unreliable.  The second axes — as you noted — are the primary axes orthogonal to the major axes of covariation between the data sets; i.e., they are not the major axes of covariation.  It is possible that if you had some kind of signal in the first axes that there might be something to also investigate in the second axes, but it you move to the second axes because the first axes did not reveal to you the signal you yearn to see, then any pattern you see in the second axes is sure to be spurious.  This is foolhardy.  You risk making improper conclusions.

Furthermore, one has to be cognizant of how much covariation is represented by the axes.  Here is a demonstration, using the example data in the phylo.integration help file:

> library(geomorph)
> data(plethspecies) 
> Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethspecies$land)    #GPA-alignment

Performing GPA
  |==============================================================================| 100%

Making projections... Finished!
> land.gps<-c("A","A","A","A","A","B","B","B","B","B","B") 
> 
> IT<- phylo.integration(Y.gpa$coords,partition.gp=land.gps,
+                        phy=plethspecies$phy,iter=999)
Random PLS calculations: 1000 permutations.

|==============================================================================| 100%

>        
> ord <- ordinate(IT$YScores, A = IT$XScores)
> round(ord$RV, 4)
 Comp1  Comp2  Comp3  Comp4  Comp5  Comp6  Comp7  Comp8  Comp9   <NA> 
0.5950 0.0545 0.0455 0.0144 0.0045 0.0004 0.0002 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 

What this means is that the amount of covariation between the data sets (modules) explained by the first PLS axes is 59.5% of the joint variation.  The second set of axes only explains 5.45%.  So are the second axes worth interpreting?  Is the "biological reality" shown by those axes biologically significant?  I doubt it.

When I excluded one of the two species that were at both ends of the PLS1 plot from my analysis, I did not observe any clusters in PLS1. In other words, could the clusters seen in this case be artificial, originating from taxon sampling, etc.?　 Incidentally, the shape change captured by PLS1 (except for one species) is similar to the shape change captured by PLS2 in the previous case.

What you did was exclude an outlier that had impressive leverage on the first axis,  but beware if it is really an outlier.  I think you missed the point of my original example.  When all taxa had a value of 0, then a value of 0.1 became an outlier.  You presented evidence that the trait does not change much on the phylogeny (a tree that was nearly completely green, rather than a combination of red, green, and blue).  This result screams to you that there is not much variation in shape.  I believe — without better evidence — you are compelled to seek a “biological reality” that does not exist.

Partial least-squares is math and this math does not have an agenda to reveal hidden information.  Like any correlation analysis, it can easily produce what seems to be impressive results, especially when looking at a plot. But you might have to use other bits of information to understand if you are being dissuaded by what your eyes see.  I recommend using the component by component RV scores as I did in the last two lines of code above.  This is not a test, like performed on the r-pls coefficient, but it might help you realize if a test is appropriate.

Hope that helps!

Mike

Sincerely, 
Naoto Toyoda

2022年1月4日火曜日 21:12:50 UTC+9 Michael Collyer:
Dear Naoto,

In PLS2, I got a not strange plot (i.e., not a centralized clusters plot) as I saw in PLS1. Is it correct to assume that PLS2 captures the "biological reality" of co-variation between traits, even though the value of the correlation coefficient is weaker than PLS1, or is this way of interpretation too simplistic, since PLS2 is constrained to be orthogonal to PLS1?

No, in absolutely no way should you feel an urge to interpret the second PLS axes as the biological reality after your first axes have proven unreliable.  The second axes — as you noted — are the primary axes orthogonal to the major axes of covariation between the data sets; i.e., they are not the major axes of covariation.  It is possible that if you had some kind of signal in the first axes that there might be something to also investigate in the second axes, but it you move to the second axes because the first axes did not reveal to you the signal you yearn to see, then any pattern you see in the second axes is sure to be spurious.  This is foolhardy.  You risk making improper conclusions.

Furthermore, one has to be cognizant of how much covariation is represented by the axes.  Here is a demonstration, using the example data in the phylo.integration help file:

> library(geomorph)
> data(plethspecies) 
> Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethspecies$land)    #GPA-alignment

Performing GPA
  |==============================================================================| 100%

Making projections... Finished!
> land.gps<-c("A","A","A","A","A","B","B","B","B","B","B") 
> 
> IT<- phylo.integration(Y.gpa$coords,partition.gp=land.gps,
+                        phy=plethspecies$phy,iter=999)

Random PLS calculations: 1000 permutations.
  |==============================================================================| 100%

>        
> ord <- ordinate(IT$YScores, A = IT$XScores)
> round(ord$RV, 4)
 Comp1  Comp2  Comp3  Comp4  Comp5  Comp6  Comp7  Comp8  Comp9   <NA> 
0.5950 0.0545 0.0455 0.0144 0.0045 0.0004 0.0002 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 

What this means is that the amount of covariation between the data sets (modules) explained by the first PLS axes is 59.5% of the joint variation.  The second set of axes only explains 5.45%.  So are the second axes worth interpreting?  Is the "biological reality" shown by those axes biologically significant?  I doubt it.


When I excluded one of the two species that were at both ends of the PLS1 plot from my analysis, I did not observe any clusters in PLS1. In other words, could the clusters seen in this case be artificial, originating from taxon sampling, etc.?　 Incidentally, the shape change captured by PLS1 (except for one species) is similar to the shape change captured by PLS2 in the previous case.

What you did was exclude an outlier that had impressive leverage on the first axis,  but beware if it is really an outlier.  I think you missed the point of my original example.  When all taxa had a value of 0, then a value of 0.1 became an outlier.  You presented evidence that the trait does not change much on the phylogeny (a tree that was nearly completely green, rather than a combination of red, green, and blue).  This result screams to you that there is not much variation in shape.  I believe — without better evidence — you are compelled to seek a “biological reality” that does not exist.

Partial least-squares is math and this math does not have an agenda to reveal hidden information.  Like any correlation analysis, it can easily produce what seems to be impressive results, especially when looking at a plot. But you might have to use other bits of information to understand if you are being dissuaded by what your eyes see.  I recommend using the component by component RV scores as I did in the last two lines of code above.  This is not a test, like performed on the r-pls coefficient, but it might help you realize if a test is appropriate.

Hope that helps!

Mike 


Sincerely, 
Naoto Toyoda

2022年1月3日月曜日 21:50:49 UTC+9 Michael Collyer:
Dear Naoto,

PLS is a correlation analysis and the pitfalls of measuring correlation are well-noted on various disciplines.  Here is recent example paper in clinical science, but others can be found for specific disciplines:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5079093/

Here is an example script that covers two problems: range of data and outliers:


> library(phytools)
> library(geomorph)
> set.seed(2003)
> tree <- pbtree(n = 12)
> plot(tree)
> 
> sisters <- c(8, 9) # sister species found in the tree for t11 and t12
> x <- y <- rep(0, 12)
> names(x) <- names(y) <- tree$tip.label
> 
> x[sisters] <- c(-0.1, 0.1)
> y[sisters] <- c(-0.2, 0.3)
> 
> PLS <- phylo.integration(x, y, phy = tree)

Random PLS calculations: 1000 permutations.
  |=============================================================================| 100%

> PLS

Call:
phylo.integration(A = x, A2 = y, phy = tree) 



r-PLS: 1

Effect Size (Z): 3.0727

P-value: 0.008

Based on 1000 random permutations
> plot(PLS, label = tree$tip.label)


This example should demonstrate that a whole lot of nothing going on can produce impressive results.  I simulated data to be practically 0 for every taxon (all were 0, two were tweaked to be practically 0).  This seems plausible with your phylogeny with trait values mapped, showing mostly invariance among all taxa.  The values that were near 0 in my simulation but not quite 0 — i.e., not the same as all others — appear to be outliers even though the range of data suggests all taxa could be considered to have practically the same value.

In other words, a correlation analysis is not warranted.

The problem above is also exacerbated by small sample size, which it appears you have.  One other clue in your data is that the estimated ancestral states are all rather clumped near 0, 0, suggesting there simply is no signal in your data to consider.  It appears all of your taxa have approximately the same shape, at least after accounting for phylogeny.

Hope that helps!

Mike

parts:
Dear Naoto, and everyone,

Since 2019 I have become increasingly more opinionated about what phylogenetic correction should mean and how it is different from what it has meant over the last few years.  I’ll assert my opinion first, and then explain.  Phylo-PCA as introduced by Liam Revell is not a phylogenetic correction method (which he states in his 2009 article, but maybe not forcefully enough to dissuade people).

Many of my following points are made in our recent MEE article for phylogenetically aligned component analysis (PACA), link here.  Just about any kind of ordination method can be thought of as a singular value decomposition (SVD) of

t(A)Z

where A in alignment matrix, t() means its transpose, and Z is a matrix of potentially transformed data, for the data matrix, Y; i.e., Z = f(Y).  Principal component analysis (PCA) can be represented this way.  In this case, A is a p x p identity matrix, for p variables.  2B-PLS is represented this way, where A is one matrix of centered data and Z is another matrix of centered data.

The left (U) and right vectors (V) of PLS, along with a diagonal matrix of singular values, D, are found via SVD as

UDt(V) = t(A)Z

If this is for PCA, V is a matrix of principal components.  D is not the matrix of eigenvalues but is easily transformed to eigenvalues by a simple calculation.  (This is how R performs PCA with prcomp — much faster than actually obtaining the covariance matrix.)  If this is done for PLS, V is the matrix of right vectors, and U is the matrix of left vectors, corresponding to the two sets of data.  This is what we do in our PLS functions in geomorph.  For PACA, A is a phylogenetic covariance matrix, and Z is either centered data or phylogenetically transformed data (more below).

And, as we show in our article, this approach can be used for phylo-PCA, in which case A is an identity matrix and Z is a transformed version of the data, based on the phylogenetic covariance matrix (C).  We show that a Cholesky decomposition (or symmetric transformation) can be performed such that C = t(T)T, with T being the transformation matrix.  If we let Z = T^-1(Y - E(Y)), where ^-1 means matrix inverse and E(Y) is the phylogenetic mean (expected value of Y), and plug this into the SVD of t(A)Z, then V is the matrix of phylo-PCs, the same as those Revell described.  PC scores are found — as Revell introduced it — via projection of data as:

P = (Y - E(Y))V

And this is why phylo-PCA DOES NOT correct for phylogeny.  This is merely a rotation of the data space to an axis other than the axis of major variation.  The first component is the component most independent of phylogeny, but again, as we show in our article, the data has the same phylogenetic signal (pushed to lower dimensions) and as Revell espoused, PGLS still needs to be performed if using P instead of Y as data.

However, if one were to do this:

P = ZV

meaning the residuals are not Z = (Y - E(Y)) but are the transformed residuals Z = T^-1(Y - E(Y)), then the ordination DOES correct for phylogeny.  Hypothetically, one should be able to perform OLS analyses on P and trust the data are rather devoid of phylogenetic signal.  For certain, the variance of PC scores following this kind of projection is the same as the variance calculated in PGLS, and the axes are truly orthogonal, compared to the correlated axes in phylo-PCA.

So my thoughts are that the problems pointed out by Polly et al. and seconded by us can be abated by performing phylo-PCA with projection of transformed residuals, rather that projection of centered values, as proposed by Revell.  While we agreed with Polly et al. in 2019, we addressed the issue more in 2021.  There are pros and cons to either approach.  The one I just mentioned is that using transformed residuals  as part of phylo-PCA actually corrects for phylogeny in the projection; phylo-PCA as it is generally used, does not.  But phylo-PCA gives you a visualization of the data space; using transformed residuals gives you a visualization of a transformed data space.

In summary, to perform phylo-PCA (Revell, 2009) and claim the data have been phylogenetically corrected, is incorrect.  To perform it with transformed residuals (Collyer and Adams, 2021) and claim the obtained scores have been phylogenetically corrected is correct, but to plot these scores and call them a representation of the data space is incorrect.

Cheers!
Mike

Dear Naoto, and everyone,

Since 2019 I have become increasingly more opinionated about what phylogenetic correction should mean and how it is different from what it has meant over the last few years.  I’ll assert my opinion first, and then explain.  Phylo-PCA as introduced by Liam Revell is not a phylogenetic correction method (which he states in his 2009 article, but maybe not forcefully enough to dissuade people).

Many of my following points are made in our recent MEE article for phylogenetically aligned component analysis (PACA), link here.  Just about any kind of ordination method can be thought of as a singular value decomposition (SVD) of

t(A)Z

where A in alignment matrix, t() means its transpose, and Z is a matrix of potentially transformed data, for the data matrix, Y; i.e., Z = f(Y).  Principal component analysis (PCA) can be represented this way.  In this case, A is a p x p identity matrix, for p variables.  2B-PLS is represented this way, where A is one matrix of centered data and Z is another matrix of centered data.

The left (U) and right vectors (V) of PLS, along with a diagonal matrix of singular values, D, are found via SVD as

UDt(V) = t(A)Z

If this is for PCA, V is a matrix of principal components.  D is not the matrix of eigenvalues but is easily transformed to eigenvalues by a simple calculation.  (This is how R performs PCA with prcomp — much faster than actually obtaining the covariance matrix.)  If this is done for PLS, V is the matrix of right vectors, and U is the matrix of left vectors, corresponding to the two sets of data.  This is what we do in our PLS functions in geomorph.  For PACA, A is a phylogenetic covariance matrix, and Z is either centered data or phylogenetically transformed data (more below).

And, as we show in our article, this approach can be used for phylo-PCA, in which case A is an identity matrix and Z is a transformed version of the data, based on the phylogenetic covariance matrix (C).  We show that a Cholesky decomposition (or symmetric transformation) can be performed such that C = t(T)T, with T being the transformation matrix.  If we let Z = T^-1(Y - E(Y)), where ^-1 means matrix inverse and E(Y) is the phylogenetic mean (expected value of Y), and plug this into the SVD of t(A)Z, then V is the matrix of phylo-PCs, the same as those Revell described.  PC scores are found — as Revell introduced it — via projection of data as:

P = (Y - E(Y))V

And this is why phylo-PCA DOES NOT correct for phylogeny.  This is merely a rotation of the data space to an axis other than the axis of major variation.  The first component is the component most independent of phylogeny, but again, as we show in our article, the data has the same phylogenetic signal (pushed to lower dimensions) and as Revell espoused, PGLS still needs to be performed if using P instead of Y as data.

However, if one were to do this:

P = ZV

meaning the residuals are not Z = (Y - E(Y)) but are the transformed residuals Z = T^-1(Y - E(Y)), then the ordination DOES correct for phylogeny.  Hypothetically, one should be able to perform OLS analyses on P and trust the data are rather devoid of phylogenetic signal.  For certain, the variance of PC scores following this kind of projection is the same as the variance calculated in PGLS, and the axes are truly orthogonal, compared to the correlated axes in phylo-PCA.

So my thoughts are that the problems pointed out by Polly et al. and seconded by us can be abated by performing phylo-PCA with projection of transformed residuals, rather that projection of centered values, as proposed by Revell.  While we agreed with Polly et al. in 2019, we addressed the issue more in 2021.  There are pros and cons to either approach.  The one I just mentioned is that using transformed residuals  as part of phylo-PCA actually corrects for phylogeny in the projection; phylo-PCA as it is generally used, does not.  But phylo-PCA gives you a visualization of the data space; using transformed residuals gives you a visualization of a transformed data space.

In summary, to perform phylo-PCA (Revell, 2009) and claim the data have been phylogenetically corrected, is incorrect.  To perform it with transformed residuals (Collyer and Adams, 2021) and claim the obtained scores have been phylogenetically corrected is correct, but to plot these scores and call them a representation of the data space is incorrect.

Cheers!
Mike

Dear Naoto,

In PLS2, I got a not strange plot (i.e., not a centralized clusters plot) as I saw in PLS1. Is it correct to assume that PLS2 captures the "biological reality" of co-variation between traits, even though the value of the correlation coefficient is weaker than PLS1, or is this way of interpretation too simplistic, since PLS2 is constrained to be orthogonal to PLS1?

No, in absolutely no way should you feel an urge to interpret the second PLS axes as the biological reality after your first axes have proven unreliable.  The second axes — as you noted — are the primary axes orthogonal to the major axes of covariation between the data sets; i.e., they are not the major axes of covariation.  It is possible that if you had some kind of signal in the first axes that there might be something to also investigate in the second axes, but it you move to the second axes because the first axes did not reveal to you the signal you yearn to see, then any pattern you see in the second axes is sure to be spurious.  This is foolhardy.  You risk making improper conclusions.

Furthermore, one has to be cognizant of how much covariation is represented by the axes.  Here is a demonstration, using the example data in the phylo.integration help file:

> library(geomorph)
> data(plethspecies) 
> Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethspecies$land)    #GPA-alignment

Performing GPA
  |==============================================================================| 100%

Making projections... Finished!
> land.gps<-c("A","A","A","A","A","B","B","B","B","B","B") 
> 
> IT<- phylo.integration(Y.gpa$coords,partition.gp=land.gps,
+                        phy=plethspecies$phy,iter=999)

Random PLS calculations: 1000 permutations.
  |==============================================================================| 100%

>        
> ord <- ordinate(IT$YScores, A = IT$XScores)
> round(ord$RV, 4)
 Comp1  Comp2  Comp3  Comp4  Comp5  Comp6  Comp7  Comp8  Comp9   <NA> 
0.5950 0.0545 0.0455 0.0144 0.0045 0.0004 0.0002 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 

What this means is that the amount of covariation between the data sets (modules) explained by the first PLS axes is 59.5% of the joint variation.  The second set of axes only explains 5.45%.  So are the second axes worth interpreting?  Is the "biological reality" shown by those axes biologically significant?  I doubt it.


When I excluded one of the two species that were at both ends of the PLS1 plot from my analysis, I did not observe any clusters in PLS1. In other words, could the clusters seen in this case be artificial, originating from taxon sampling, etc.?　 Incidentally, the shape change captured by PLS1 (except for one species) is similar to the shape change captured by PLS2 in the previous case.

What you did was exclude an outlier that had impressive leverage on the first axis,  but beware if it is really an outlier.  I think you missed the point of my original example.  When all taxa had a value of 0, then a value of 0.1 became an outlier.  You presented evidence that the trait does not change much on the phylogeny (a tree that was nearly completely green, rather than a combination of red, green, and blue).  This result screams to you that there is not much variation in shape.  I believe — without better evidence — you are compelled to seek a “biological reality” that does not exist.

Partial least-squares is math and this math does not have an agenda to reveal hidden information.  Like any correlation analysis, it can easily produce what seems to be impressive results, especially when looking at a plot. But you might have to use other bits of information to understand if you are being dissuaded by what your eyes see.  I recommend using the component by component RV scores as I did in the last two lines of code above.  This is not a test, like performed on the r-pls coefficient, but it might help you realize if a test is appropriate.

Hope that helps!

Dear Naoto,

PLS is a correlation analysis and the pitfalls of measuring correlation are well-noted on various disciplines.  Here is recent example paper in clinical science, but others can be found for specific disciplines:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5079093/

Here is an example script that covers two problems: range of data and outliers:


> library(phytools)
> library(geomorph)
> set.seed(2003)
> tree <- pbtree(n = 12)
> plot(tree)
> 
> sisters <- c(8, 9) # sister species found in the tree for t11 and t12
> x <- y <- rep(0, 12)
> names(x) <- names(y) <- tree$tip.label
> 
> x[sisters] <- c(-0.1, 0.1)
> y[sisters] <- c(-0.2, 0.3)
> 
> PLS <- phylo.integration(x, y, phy = tree)

Random PLS calculations: 1000 permutations.
  |=============================================================================| 100%

> PLS

Call:
phylo.integration(A = x, A2 = y, phy = tree) 



r-PLS: 1

Effect Size (Z): 3.0727

P-value: 0.008

Based on 1000 random permutations
> plot(PLS, label = tree$tip.label)


This example should demonstrate that a whole lot of nothing going on can produce impressive results.  I simulated data to be practically 0 for every taxon (all were 0, two were tweaked to be practically 0).  This seems plausible with your phylogeny with trait values mapped, showing mostly invariance among all taxa.  The values that were near 0 in my simulation but not quite 0 — i.e., not the same as all others — appear to be outliers even though the range of data suggests all taxa could be considered to have practically the same value.

In other words, a correlation analysis is not warranted.

The problem above is also exacerbated by small sample size, which it appears you have.  One other clue in your data is that the estimated ancestral states are all rather clumped near 0, 0, suggesting there simply is no signal in your data to consider.  It appears all of your taxa have approximately the same shape, at least after accounting for phylogeny.

Hope that helps!

Mike
